'''''Tomorrow Never Dies''''' is a 1999 [[third-person shooter]] video game developed by [[Black Ops Entertainment]] and co-published by [[Electronic Arts]] and [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer|MGM Interactive]] for the [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]]. It is based on the 1997 [[James Bond]] film ''[[Tomorrow Never Dies]]''.

Development began in 1997, before the film's release. The game's storyline was originally meant to pick up after the events of the film, but this was scrapped following feedback from [[focus group]]s. The game's release was delayed several times, and additional levels and a multiplayer mode were removed during development.

The game was eventually released in November 1999, the same month that the next film in the Bond series, ''[[The World Is Not Enough]]'', was released in cinemas. It is the first 007 game to be published by EA since acquiring the James Bond licence. It was released following the success of another James Bond game, ''[[GoldenEye 007]]'' (1997). Critics were disappointed with ''Tomorrow Never Dies'', believing that it fell short of the previous game, although the soundtrack was praised.

== Gameplay ==
[[File:Tommorow Never Dies.jpg|thumb|left|Screenshot of a wounded Bond outside a Russian military outpost]]
''Tomorrow Never Dies'' is a [[third-person shooter]] with elements of [[Stealth game|stealth]] gameplay. [[MI6]] agent James Bond is the player character for most of the game, and Chinese agent [[Wai Lin]] is also playable in one level. The player can walk, run, sneak, sidestep, and roll. A variety of weapons can be used throughout the game, including a sniper rifle. The game switches to a first-person perspective when aiming weapons.<ref name=GF /><ref name=IGN /><ref name=GPro /><ref name=DR />

Clips from the film are shown after each level to advance the story. The game is played across ten levels, two of which include a skiing portion. Another level is played primarily as a driving game, with the player using an armed car to destroy enemy vehicles.<ref name=GF /><ref name=IGN /><ref name=GPro /><ref name=DR>{{cite web |last=O'Connor |first=Frank |title=Tomorrow Never Dies Preview |url=http://www.dailyradar.com/previews/game_preview_7.html |website=[[Daily Radar]] |publisher=[[Future US|Imagine Media]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010804142329/http://www.dailyradar.com/previews/game_preview_7.html |archive-date=4 August 2001}}</ref>

== Plot ==
The game's plot closely follows that of the [[Tomorrow Never Dies|film]]. Bond begins to cross the [[China–Russia border]] into a Russian radar base, which is intercepting messages delicate in subject. Using a [[laser designator]], Bond targets the dish and a British jet flies over, dropping an air-to-surface missile. A helicopter arrives, and Bond kills the occupants and recovers a key. He uses the key to unlock a large gate and makes his escape on [[skis]]. Bond reaches the end of the run – a sheer cliff drop. Bond continues, and opens his [[Union Jack]] [[parachute]].

Bond later lands in an arms bazaar. After taking photographs of military hardware, a British naval ship launches a [[BGM-109 Tomahawk]] to eliminate all potential threats and hardware. Bond realizes there are [[nuclear weapons]] at the Bazaar on a [[L-39 Albatros]] jet. After an intense firefight between Bond and Russian terrorists, he hijacks the jet and returns to [[Secret Intelligence Service|MI6]].

Bond is sent to investigate a man called [[Elliot Carver]] during a party in [[Hamburg]], [[Germany]] after a British warship sank in the [[South China Sea]], with all hands going down. Carver Media published the full story before MI6 received a full report, raising MI6's suspicions. During the party Bond meets his former lover, Paris, now Carver's wife, who slaps him. Carver arrives, and offers a "tour of the facilities". Bond follows, but is knocked out by a henchman. He wakes up in a room with a large 2-way mirror. He uses his laser-[[cufflinks]] to escape, then he destroys the central computer, allowing him to make his escape. He then makes his way to the press and engages in a firefight between Carver's guards.

He recovers Henry Gupta's GPS scrambler, which was used to lure the British navy into Chinese waters to try and spark an international incident. As the existing Chinese government is not receptive to giving Carver Media Group Network exclusive broadcast rights in China, Carver plans to start a war to eliminate the present government and replace it with politicians more supportive of his plans. Bond then escapes to the Hotel Atlantic, where Paris is being held prisoner. He arrives, and heads to the bar where he asks to see Paris; resulting in a shootout between Bond and the guards, who were working for Carver. Bond uses the elevator to get to Paris' apartment, where he meets Kaufman. Kaufman tries to kill Bond by using spinning razor discs and an [[AK-47]]. Bond kills Kaufman and helps Paris escape. They go to the underground garage, where Bond drives away in his [[BMW 7 Series (E38)|BMW 7 Series]].

MI6 has found the headquarters of Henry Gupta near the foothills of the [[Swiss Alps]]. The convoy of terrorist cars and trucks is heading to Gupta's Alpine hideout for an important meeting. Bond is sent to stop the convoy. Along the way, Bond meets Q, who gives him the BMW to stop the convoy. Bond successfully destroys the convoy with the BMW and drives away. Bond is then sent to a ski ridge in [[Hokkaido]], [[Japan]], to track down and kill chemical expert Satoshi Isagura, who is thought to be working for Elliot Carver after a nerve gas attack in [[Yokohama]].  Carver Media was also the first to report the story. Bond kills Isagura and is sent to [[Ho Chi Minh City|Saigon]].

Bond steals a data disk from Carver Media Tower in Saigon but is captured. Bond manages to escape with the data disk. The next night, Carver bribes the Saigon [[Military Police]] to kill Bond on sight, so MI6 pulls Bond out as the mission would be compromised were Bond to be seen or killed. Bond gives [[Wai Lin]] the data disk, and Wai Lin engages the Saigon Military Police in a gun battle with the police setting roadblocks and using fast-firing chain guns. She makes it back to her lab to find the location of Carter's [[stealth boat]], hidden in [[Hạ Long Bay]]. On the stealth boat, Bond uses the boat's commlink to give MI6 its position. Wai Lin is kidnapped but is later freed by Bond after he kills Carver's right-hand man, Stamper. Wai Lin stops the engine while Bond shoots and kills Carver and stops the stolen [[nuclear missile]] from destroying [[Beijing]]. Bond and Wai Lin escape the stealth boat before it self-destructs.

== Development ==
Before the 1997 release of the film, [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer|MGM Interactive]] approached [[Black Ops Entertainment]] about developing a video game adaptation. Early development was already underway by the time that another James Bond game, ''[[GoldenEye 007|GoldenEye]]'', had been released. Black Ops CEO John Botti said that ''GoldenEye'' "raised the bar for video gaming in general, but our different platform and movie inspiration destined us to make a different game – one specifically for the PlayStation – with a similar but different Bond experience".<ref>{{cite web |date=2 July 1999 |title=Tomorrow Never Dies Designer Diary (page 1 of 7) |url=http://videogames.gamespot.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/070299/index.html |website=VideoGames.com |publisher=Ziff Davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20001016000034/http://videogames.gamespot.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/070299/index.html |archive-date=16 October 2000}}</ref> The skiing and driving portions, along with the third-person perspective, were added to distinguish the game from ''GoldenEye'', a first-person shooter which lacked such gameplay elements.<ref name=preE3 />

As work began on the game, Botti watched all of the James Bond films released up to that point.<ref>{{cite web |date=2 July 1999 |title=Tomorrow Never Dies Designer Diary (page 4 of 7) |url=http://videogames.gamespot.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/070299/page4.html |website=VideoGames.com |publisher=Ziff Davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010116222000/http://videogames.gamespot.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/070299/page4.html |archive-date=16 January 2001}}</ref> For the sake of gameplay, the game includes some differences from the film such as skiing,<ref name=OUSPM1>{{cite magazine |title=Previews: Tomorrow Never Dies |url=https://archive.org/details/Official_US_PlayStation_Magazine_Volume_2_Issue_9_1999-06_Ziff_Davis_US/page/n57/mode/2up |magazine=[[Official U.S. PlayStation Magazine]] |publisher=Ziff Davis |location=United States |volume=2 |issue=9 |date=June 1999 |page=58 |access-date=7 October 2023}}</ref><ref name=preE3 /> a feature that Black Ops was intent on adding. Scuba diving had also been planned.<ref name=GS1999>{{cite web |author=GameSpot staff |date=8 June 1999 |title=Tomorrow Never Dies (Preview) |url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/tomorrow-never-dies/1100-2323277/ |website=GameSpot |publisher=Fandom |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151231030937/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/tomorrow-never-dies/1100-2323277/ |archive-date=31 December 2015 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=10 August 1999 |title=Tomorrow Never Dies Designer Diary (page 1 of 2) |url=http://videogames.gamespot.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/081099/index.html |website=VideoGames.com |publisher=Ziff Davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030315161822/http://videogames.gamespot.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/081099/index.html |archive-date=15 March 2003}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=2 July 1999 |title=Tomorrow Never Dies Designer Diary (page 3 of 7) |url=http://videogames.gamespot.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/070299/page3.html |website=VideoGames.com |publisher=Ziff Davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000709062438/http://videogames.gamespot.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/070299/page3.html |archive-date=9 July 2000}}</ref> Programmer Will Botti began working on the game in November 1997, and was given a short period of 30 days to create a [[game engine]] for the skiing levels. Will Botti would become the project director in April 1998.<ref>{{cite web |date=10 August 1999 |title=Tomorrow Never Dies Designer Diary (page 2 of 2) |url=http://www.videogames.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/081099/page2.html |website=VideoGames.com |publisher=Ziff Davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020606214728/http://www.videogames.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/081099/page2.html |archive-date=6 June 2002}}</ref>

The game had a development period of approximately two years.<ref>{{cite web |date=2 July 1999 |title=Tomorrow Never Dies Designer Diary (page 2 of 7) |url=http://videogames.gamespot.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/070299/page2.html |website=VideoGames.com |publisher=Ziff Davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000615144446/http://videogames.gamespot.com/features/universal/tnd_dd/070299/page2.html |archive-date=15 June 2000}}</ref> It was originally intended as a continuation of the film with a story that would have picked up where the film left off.<ref name=preE3 /><ref name=GS1999 /><ref>{{cite magazine |title=PlayStation Previews: Tomorrow Never Dies |url=https://archive.org/details/ElectronicGamingMonthly103/page/n79/mode/2up |magazine=[[Electronic Gaming Monthly]] |publisher=Ziff Davis |issue=103 |date=February 1998 |page=76 |access-date=7 October 2023}}</ref> David Bishop, president of [[MGM Home Entertainment]], said in June 1998, "We didn't see any benefit to following the script verbatim. We just felt we had more freedom in what we could bring the gaming world if we went outside the set script."<ref>{{cite web |last=Ragals |first=Dave |date=11 June 1998 |title=Lights, Camera, Interaction! |url=http://edition.cnn.com/TECH/computing/9806/11/movie.games/ |website=[[CNN]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031020163751/http://edition.cnn.com/TECH/computing/9806/11/movie.games/ |archive-date=20 October 2003 |url-status=dead}}</ref> However, [[focus group]]s were more interested in seeing familiar scenes from the film.<ref name=preE3>{{cite web |last=Perry |first=Douglass C. |date=11 May 1999 |title=Pre-E3: Tomorrow Never Dies Interview |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/1999/05/12/pre-e3-tomorrow-never-dies-interview |website=IGN |publisher=Ziff Davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211029032422/https://www.ign.com/articles/1999/05/12/pre-e3-tomorrow-never-dies-interview |archive-date=29 October 2021 |url-status=live |access-date=7 October 2023}}</ref> The game's release was delayed several times,<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Tomorrow Never Dies: At long last, James Bond makes his PlayStation debut |url=https://archive.org/details/Official_US_PlayStation_Magazine_Volume_3_Issue_2_1999-11_Ziff_Davis_US/page/n77/mode/2up |magazine=Official U.S. PlayStation Magazine |publisher=Ziff Davis |location=United States |volume=3 |issue=2 |date=November 1999 |page=78 |access-date=7 October 2023}}</ref> and was scheduled at one point for January 1999.<ref name=OUSPM1 /> Additional levels and a two-player mode were eventually removed.<ref name=Perry>{{cite web |last=Perry |first=Douglass C. |date=29 October 1999 |title=Tomorrow Never Dies (Preview) |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/1999/10/30/tomorrow-never-dies-2 |website=IGN |publisher=Ziff Davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220128105615/https://www.ign.com/articles/1999/10/30/tomorrow-never-dies-2 |archive-date=28 January 2022 |url-status=live |access-date=7 October 2023}}</ref> The latter feature was scrapped as the developers sought to focus on the single-player mode.<ref name=Perry />

In late 1998, MGM partnered with [[Electronic Arts]] to co-publish games such as ''Tomorrow Never Dies''.<ref>{{cite web |author=IGN staff |date=20 November 1998 |title=EA and MGM Bond |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/1998/11/21/ea-and-mgm-bond |website=IGN |publisher=Ziff Davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230412131647/https://www.ign.com/articles/1998/11/21/ea-and-mgm-bond |archive-date=12 April 2023 |url-status=live |access-date=7 October 2023}}</ref> The game was completed on 29 October 1999, and released in North America on 16 November, and in the United Kingdom on 25 November.<ref name=Perry /><ref>{{cite web |author=IGN staff |date=16 November 1999 |title=Woody, Buzz, Jordan and Bond All Now on PlayStation |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/1999/11/17/woody-buzz-jordan-and-bond-all-now-on-playstation |website=IGN |publisher=Ziff Davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322121036/https://www.ign.com/articles/1999/11/17/woody-buzz-jordan-and-bond-all-now-on-playstation |archive-date=22 March 2023 |url-status=live |access-date=7 October 2023}}</ref><ref name="uk" />

The game includes voice-acting, although none of the film's actors reprised their roles.<ref name=OUSPM1 /> The game's musical score was composed by [[Tommy Tallarico]], and was released separately as ''Tomorrow Never Dies The Original Soundtrack from the Videogame''. It includes 16 tracks written for the game and a bonus track.<ref name=Rockin>{{cite web |author=IGN staff |date=18 February 2000 |title=Rockin' Bond Videogame Soundtrack |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2000/02/19/rockin-bond-videogame-soundtrack |website=IGN |publisher=Ziff Davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211113182450/https://www.ign.com/articles/2000/02/19/rockin-bond-videogame-soundtrack |archive-date=13 November 2021 |url-status=live |access-date=7 October 2023}}</ref>

The game received mixed reviews according to the [[Review aggregator|review aggregation]] website [[GameRankings]].<ref name=GR /> Adam Pavlacka of ''[[Next Generation (magazine)|NextGen]]'' said of the game, "Take away the Bond license, and what's left is a very basic third-person shooter with little innovation."<ref name=NGen /> In Japan, where the game was ported and published by [[Square (video game company)#Publishing and subsidiaries|Electronic Arts Square]] on 10 February 2000, ''[[Famitsu]]'' gave it a score of 27 out of 40.<ref name=Fam />

Following the success of ''GoldenEye'', critics were disappointed with ''Tomorrow Never Dies'', believing that it fell far short of the previous game.<ref name=AG /><ref name=GF /><ref name=GPro /><ref name=GameRev /><ref name=GS /><ref name=IGN /><ref name=NGen /> Rick Mears of ''[[GameFan]]'' wrote that after ''GoldenEye'', "did we really ever expect anything to come close?"<ref name=GF /> ''[[IGN]]''{{'}}s Douglass C. Perry wrote, "Despite wanting to avoid comparisons, it's nearly impossible for TND to shake the legacy of ''Goldeneye''".<ref name=IGN /> Uncle Dust of ''[[GamePro]]'' wrote in one review, "Unfortunate comparisons to ''Goldeneye'' will probably occur, and to that ''Tomorrow Never Dies'' is an inferior game. But on its own ''TND'' gives you great Bond-style thrills in a less-than-polished package."<ref name=GPro>{{cite magazine |author=Uncle Dust |date=20 November 1999 |title=Tomorrow Never Dies Review for PlayStation from GamePro.com |url=http://www.gamepro.com/sony/psx/games/reviews/3232.shtml |magazine=[[GamePro]] |publisher=[[International Data Group|IDG]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040315064923/http://gamepro.com/sony/psx/games/reviews/3232.shtml |archive-date=15 March 2004 |access-date=12 December 2013}}</ref>{{efn|''[[GamePro]]'' gave the game two 3.5/5 scores for graphics and fun factor, 3/5 for sound, and 4.5/5 for control in one review.}} In another ''GamePro'' review, Air Hendrix said, "You can't beat the marquee value of ''007'', so ''TND'' is worth renting to check its license to kill—even if there is no multiplayer action. Still, ''Tomorrow Never Dies'' is no ''GoldenEye'', and gamers have come to expect much more from ''Bond''."<ref>{{cite magazine |author=Air Hendrix |title=007: Tomorrow Never Dies |url=https://retrocdn.net/images/8/81/GamePro_US_136.pdf |magazine=GamePro |publisher=IDG |issue=136 |date=January 2000 |page=88 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230708183932/https://retrocdn.net/images/8/81/GamePro_US_136.pdf |archive-date=8 July 2023 |url-status=live |access-date=8 October 2023}}</ref>{{efn|''[[GamePro]]'' gave the game two 3.5/5 scores for graphics and fun factor, 4.5/5 for sound, and 2.5/5 for control in another review.}} Scott Alan Marriott, writing for ''[[AllGame]]'', felt that the game lacked the polishing that would be expected considering its delays. He concluded that the game "makes you appreciate GoldenEye that much more".<ref name=AG /> Joe Fielder of ''[[GameSpot]]'' stated that unlike ''GoldenEye'', each mission in ''Tomorrow Never Dies'' "ends on an anticlimactic note, making you think, 'Oh, it's over?'"<ref name=GS />

The game received comparisons to ''[[Syphon Filter (video game)|Syphon Filter]]'', which some critics deemed superior.<ref name=AG /><ref name=GF /><ref name=GI /><ref name=GameRev /><ref name=GS /> The [[Artificial intelligence in video games|artificial intelligence]] was criticized,<ref name=AG /><ref name=GPro /><ref name=GameRev /><ref name=GS /> as was the game's short length.<ref name=GS /><ref name=GameRev /><ref name=GPro /><ref name=IGN /><ref name=NGen /> Critics also complained of problems such as clipping and poor [[collision detection]].<ref name=AG /><ref name=GF /><ref name=GPro /><ref name=GameRev /><ref name=IGN /> Mears stated that walls "become translucent" and "bad guys appear out of nowhere".<ref name=GF /> The game also received some criticism for its lack of multiplayer.<ref name=AG /><ref name=IGN />

Marriott found the film-based clips to be short and of little value,<ref name=AG /> while Johnny Liu of ''[[GameRevolution]]'' wrote that much of the film footage "just doesn't flow because of the game's choppy graphics".<ref name=GameRev />

The camera and controls were criticized as well.<ref name=AG /><ref name=GI /><ref name=GF /><ref name=IGN /> Justin Braxton-Brown, writing for ''[[The Cincinnati Enquirer]]'', complained of Bond's slow running speed. He also stated that when Bond "attempts a 180-degree turn to face an adversary, gamers end up being shot in the back several times or spinning too far and being shot while trying to locate the enemy Bond just spun past".<ref name=Cin /> Perry stated that "even walking over simple power-ups can be a task".<ref name=IGN /> Marriott complained of Bond's limited moves, noting that he cannot jump, climb, or crawl.<ref name=AG />

Mears commended the game for its inclusion of skiing and driving portions, but also considered them "passable at best",<ref name=GF /> while Marriott praised them.<ref name=AG /> Perry found the car level to be uninspired and considered the skiing portions to be "the biggest area of missed opportunities".<ref name=IGN /> Liu stated that these portions of the game "aren't very well done and don't add much. They're really just there to proclaim variety".<ref name=GameRev />

The soundtrack was praised by critics,<ref name=GI /><ref name=GF /><ref name=GPro /><ref name=GameRev /><ref name=IGN /> with Mears calling it the game's most "astounding" feature.<ref name=GF /> ''IGN'' called it "a much better value than the horrible excuse for a PlayStation game that it's from".<ref name=Rockin />

The game received a "Platinum" sales award from the [[The Association for UK Interactive Entertainment|Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association]] (ELSPA),<ref>{{cite web |title=ELSPA Sales Awards: Platinum |url=http://www.elspa.com/?i=3944 |website=[[The Association for UK Interactive Entertainment|Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090515224703/http://www.elspa.com/?i=3944 |archive-date=15 May 2009}}</ref> indicating sales of at least 300,000 units in the UK.<ref>{{cite web |last=Caoili |first=Eric |date=26 November 2008 |title=ELSPA: Wii Fit, Mario Kart Reach Diamond Status In UK |url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/pc/elspa-i-wii-fit-mario-kart-i-reach-diamond-status-in-uk |website=[[Game Developer (website)|Game Developer]] |publisher=[[Informa]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170918063107/https://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/112220/ELSPA_Wii_Fit_Mario_Kart_Reach_Diamond_Status_In_UK.php |archive-date=18 September 2017 |url-status=live |access-date=8 October 2023}}</ref>
